about: Simulator: one gene with two alleles in a population of N diploid adults: Hardy-Weinberg expectations, genetic drift (Wright-Fisher sampling with a seeded generator), selection, mutation, migration, non-random mating (inbreeding) and a bottleneck or founder event, over many generations in replicate populations. Model code: bio/assets/tools/bio-tool-math.js (ApBioMath.popgen, seeded with ApBioMath.rng). Validator: scripts/lib/apbio-tool-checks/hardy-weinberg-drift.mjs checks each rule through the model (equilibrium with no forces, selection against aa, heterozygote advantage, mutation and migration equilibria, inbreeding, unbiased and reproducible drift that is faster in small populations, the bottleneck) and recomputes every number in the stimulus tables, including the seeded runs, and the numeric answer.
intro: Follow one gene with two alleles, A and a, through many generations. Choose the population size, then add selection, mutation, migrants or non-random mating, and run several populations side by side. Watch the frequency of A wander, settle or vanish, compare each generation's genotypes with the Hardy-Weinberg expectation, and test the difference with chi-square. Every random run comes from a seed you can see and type, so anyone with the same seed gets the same result. The questions below use the same model.
howItWorks:
The gene has two alleles: A, with frequency p, and a, with frequency q = 1 − p. Each individual is AA, Aa or aa. If nothing changes the allele frequencies and mating is random, the genotypes settle at the Hardy-Weinberg frequencies p², 2pq and q², and p stays the same from one generation to the next.

p + q = 1 · p² + 2pq + q² = 1

Each generation the model takes these steps, in this order:

  1. Selection. Each genotype has a fitness from 0 to 1: its share of offspring compared with the others. An aa fitness of 0 means aa individuals leave no offspring. The adults' alleles are counted into the gene pool in proportion to their genotype's fitness.
  2. Mutation. A fraction u of A alleles in the gene pool become a, and a fraction v of a alleles become A.
  3. Migration (gene flow). A fraction m of the gene pool is replaced by alleles from migrants, whose frequency of A is the donor p.
  4. Mating. With random mating the new zygotes are p², 2pq and q². Non-random mating is set by F, the share of matings between relatives: it makes AA p²(1 − F) + pF, Aa 2pq(1 − F) and aa q²(1 − F) + qF, so there are fewer heterozygotes, but p itself does not change.
  5. Genetic drift. Only N of the zygotes become the next generation's adults, picked at random one by one (a Wright-Fisher population). By chance, the adults' allele frequency differs a little from the zygotes'. In a very large population the adults match the zygotes exactly, so there is no drift and every replicate is identical.
  • Generation 0 is set, not drawn: N adults with p as chosen and the genotypes of step 4, rounded to whole individuals, the same in every replicate.
  • Fixed and lost. When p reaches 1, A is fixed (every allele is A); when p reaches 0, A is lost. With no mutation or migration a fixed or lost allele never comes back.
  • Bottleneck and founder event. A bottleneck shrinks the population to a few adults for some generations, then it returns to N. A founder event is a one-generation bottleneck: a few individuals start a new population, which is the one the graph then follows.
  • Random numbers. The seed starts a generator that gives the same numbers every time. Replicate 1 uses the seed, and each later replicate its own stream from it, so the same seed and settings always give the same runs, and adding replicates does not change the first ones.
  • Chi-square against Hardy-Weinberg. For the generation you read, the expected counts are N·p², N·2pq and N·q², using p from the same adults. χ² = Σ (o − e)² / e. With three genotypes the usual rule gives 3 − 1 = 2 degrees of freedom (critical value 5.99 at p = 0.05); some statistics books use 1 because p was estimated from the same counts (critical value 3.84). The tool shows both decisions; when they differ, say which rule you used. With an expected count below 5 the test is unreliable.
  • Fitness, mutation and migration act on the gene pool, not on chance, so with a very large population (no drift) the model has no randomness at all.

presets.label: Hardy-Weinberg: very large population, no forces
Selection against a lethal recessive (aa fitness 0)
Bottleneck: 1000 adults, then 5 for two generations

hw-s1.title: Drift, selection and mating in a model population
hw-s1.text:
A student used the model, which follows one gene with alleles A and a. Unless stated, every population started at p = 0.5 (the frequency of A), mated at random, and had no selection, mutation or migration.

Table 1: for each population size, ten replicate populations were run for 100 generations with seed 2026; the table counts how each population ended. Table 2: a very large population (no drift) in which aa individuals leave no offspring (fitness 1, 1 and 0 for AA, Aa and aa); q is the frequency of a. Table 3: two populations of 200 adults that started at p = 0.6 and were run for 20 generations with seed 2026: population P mates at random; in population Q one mating in five is between relatives (F = 0.2). The table gives generation 20's genotype counts and the counts expected under Hardy-Weinberg from that generation's own allele frequency.

tables.caption: Table 1. Fate of allele A after 100 generations in 10 replicate populations
Table 2. Selection against aa in a very large population
Table 3. Genotype counts in generation 20 (200 adults)

questions.q: In Table 1, populations of 10 or 20 adults usually ended with one allele fixed or lost, while every population of 200 still had both alleles. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?
options: Each generation is a random sample of the previous one, and chance changes in allele frequency are larger when fewer individuals are sampled
Small populations have more mutations per individual, so one allele replaces the other faster
Natural selection is stronger in small populations, so the better allele spreads to fixation
Large populations mate at random, while small populations cannot

why.correct: With no selection, mutation or migration, the only thing changing p is chance: which individuals happen to become the next generation's adults. Sampling 20 individuals moves p much further, by chance, than sampling 200, so small populations wander to p = 0 or p = 1 within 100 generations while large ones barely move. That is genetic drift.
options: Right: drift is random sampling, and its effect is larger in smaller populations.
The runs had no mutation at all, so mutation cannot explain the difference.
The runs had no selection (every genotype had fitness 1), and A was fixed in some small populations and lost in others, which is not the pattern of one allele being favored.
Every population in Table 1 mated at random; population size changed, not the mating pattern.

questions.q: In Table 1, the populations of 20 that received 10% migrants (with p = 0.5) all kept both alleles, while most populations of 20 without migrants lost one. Which explanation is most consistent with the model?
options: Each generation the migrants bring in both alleles and pull p back toward 0.5, which undoes much of the change caused by drift
Migrants make the population mate at random, which stops drift
Migrants carry new mutations that create the missing allele again
Migration raises the fitness of heterozygotes, so both alleles are kept by selection

why.correct: Gene flow adds alleles from outside every generation. Because the migrants carry A at frequency 0.5, a population that drifts toward 0 or 1 is pulled back toward 0.5, and an allele that becomes rare is brought back in. Drift still happens, but it is balanced by gene flow, so populations stay polymorphic and more alike.
options: Right: gene flow reintroduces alleles and opposes drift.
Populations without migrants also mated at random in the model; random mating does not stop drift, because each generation is still a small sample.
There was no mutation in these runs; the migrants carry existing A and a alleles from their own population.
Every genotype had fitness 1 in these runs, so no genotype was favored; the alleles were kept by the steady inflow of migrants.

questions.q: In Table 2, aa individuals leave no offspring, yet q falls from 0.500 to 0.250 in two generations but takes another 18 generations to fall from 0.250 to 0.045. Which explanation best accounts for the slowing?
options: As q falls, most a alleles are carried by heterozygotes, which have normal fitness, so selection removes a smaller share of the a alleles each generation
The a allele mutates back to A more often when it is rare
The aa individuals become more fit as they become rare
Genetic drift adds a alleles back to the population each generation

why.correct: Selection here acts only on aa individuals. When q is 0.5, a quarter of the zygotes are aa and half of all a alleles are in them. When q is 0.1, only 1% of zygotes are aa and about 90% of a alleles sit in Aa individuals, which selection does not touch. So each generation removes a smaller fraction of the a alleles, and a harmful recessive allele lingers at low frequency.
options: Right: a recessive allele hides in heterozygotes, where selection cannot act on it.
The run in Table 2 had no mutation, so back mutation cannot explain the slowing.
The aa fitness stayed at 0 throughout; what changes is how many a alleles are in aa individuals.
The population in Table 2 is very large, so there is no drift in this run.

questions.q: Using the observed and expected counts for population Q in Table 3, calculate the chi-square value for the difference from Hardy-Weinberg expectations. Round to one decimal place.

why.correct: χ² = Σ (o − e)² / e = (85 − 71.40)² / 71.40 + (69 − 96.20)² / 96.20 + (46 − 32.40)² / 32.40 = 2.59 + 7.69 + 5.71 = 15.99, about 16.0. The largest term comes from the heterozygotes: there are 27 fewer than expected.

questions.q: Population P in Table 3 has χ² = 0.48 and population Q has χ² = 16.0 (critical value 5.99 at p = 0.05). Which conclusion is best supported by these results and the model's rules?
options: Q's genotypes differ significantly from Hardy-Weinberg expectations, with too few heterozygotes, as expected when relatives mate; P's do not differ significantly
Both populations are evolving by drift, so both are expected to differ significantly from Hardy-Weinberg expectations
Q's allele frequency must have changed by selection, because only selection changes genotype frequencies
P differs significantly from Hardy-Weinberg expectations because its counts do not exactly equal the expected counts

why.correct: Q's χ² of 16.0 is above 5.99 (and above 3.84, the value some books use), so the difference from Hardy-Weinberg is unlikely to be chance alone. The difference is a shortage of heterozygotes and an excess of both homozygotes, the signature of mating between relatives. P's χ² of 0.48 is far below the critical value, so its small differences are consistent with chance, even though drift also acts on P.
options: Right: Q departs from Hardy-Weinberg with a heterozygote shortage; P does not.
Drift changes p between generations, but with random mating each generation's genotypes are still close to p², 2pq and q² for that generation's own p, as in P.
Mating between relatives changes genotype frequencies without changing allele frequencies; there was no selection in either population.
Observed counts almost never match expected counts exactly; the chi-square test asks whether the difference is larger than chance would give, and 0.48 is not.

frq.title: Mini free-response question: drift in small and large populations

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using Table 1, describe how the number of populations that still had both alleles after 100 generations changed as population size increased, with no migrants.

rubric.point: Describes that more populations kept both alleles as N increased: 0 of 10 at N = 10, 1 at N = 20, 6 at N = 50 and all 10 at N = 200.
accept: larger populations kept both alleles more often
small populations usually fixed or lost an allele

parts.sample: As the population got larger, more populations kept both alleles: none of the ten at 10 adults, one at 20, six at 50 and all ten at 200.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why genetic drift fixes or removes alleles faster in a small population than in a large one.

rubric.point: Explains that each generation's alleles are a random sample of the previous generation's, so allele frequencies change by chance.
Explains that a smaller sample gives larger chance changes in allele frequency, so p reaches 0 or 1 sooner (and, with no mutation or migration, a lost allele cannot return).
accept: chance has a bigger effect on few individuals
a rare allele is more likely to be missed in a small sample

parts.sample: The adults of each generation are a random sample of the offspring of the one before, so by chance some alleles are passed on more often than others and p changes even with no selection. In a small population the sample is small, so these chance changes are large and p can wander to 0 or 1 within a few dozen generations. Once an allele is lost it cannot come back without mutation or migration. In a large population the chance changes are tiny, so p stays near its starting value.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A population of 1,000 adults with p = 0.5 is reduced to 5 adults for two generations, then grows back to 1,000. Predict the effect on the population's genetic variation compared with a population that stayed at 1,000, and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts less genetic variation (allele frequency shifted by chance, possibly an allele lost or fixed; fewer heterozygotes) and justifies it: drift is strong while only 5 adults pass on alleles, and the population keeps the changed frequencies when it grows back.
accept: a bottleneck reduces variation by drift
the survivors' alleles, not the original ones, fill the regrown population

parts.sample: The bottlenecked population will most likely have less genetic variation. With only 5 adults (10 alleles) for two generations, drift changes p a lot by chance and can lose one allele entirely. When the population grows back to 1,000, it carries the survivors' allele frequencies, and an allele that was lost does not return without mutation or migration. The population that stayed at 1,000 keeps p near 0.5 and both alleles.
